abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that RL and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors.

abstract: Abstract Motivation Biomedical question answering often requires evidence beyond topically retrieved literature, including gene alias resolution, database identifier normalization, and atlas-derived biological measurements. However, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically follow a fixed workflow and lack an explicit mechanism for deciding when retrieved text is sufficient, when biomedical entity mapping is needed, or when executable evidence assembly over structured measurements should be invoked. This motivates a substrate-aware large language model (LLM) harness that selectively assembles sufficient evidence by combining literature retrieval, biomedical entity mapping, and access to atlas-derived measurements. Results We introduce BioHarness, an LLM harness for staged biomedical evidence assembly across literature retrieval, biomedical entity-mapping resources, and atlas-derived structured measurements. Across 22 123 biomedical QA items spanning seven answer formats, BioHarness improves the pooled score from 62.2 to 67.2 over the strongest baseline. Ablations, case studies, and backbone-scaling analyses show that these gains arise from repairing evidence-substrate mismatches through reranking, entity grounding, and structured measurement access, rather than from indiscriminately invoking more reasoning steps, retrieving additional literature, or relying on a particular answer-model scale. Comparisons with the frontier models and harness show that BioHarness, despite using an open-weight backbone with only 3B active parameters, approaches frontier-level performance on selected literature QA tasks and outperforms frontier harnesses without web access on biomedical identifier and locus lookup. Availability and implementation The source code, reproducible benchmarking scripts, and processed benchmark data required to reproduce all results in this study are publicly available under an open-source license, together with the exat configuration, model versions, and decoding settings used in our experiments. In addition, we developed a prototype web demo (https://xcompass.scimatrix.cn/) that illustrates how BioHarness can be used in an interactive biomedical QA setting.

abstract: Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) has moved from a novelty product to mainstream consumer finance in the space of a few years. Before 2020, BNPL was a niche offering at the checkouts of online fashion merchants. BNPL then experienced substantial growth (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2022; Salem & Udis, 2025), coinciding with increased online shopping since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. BNPL is now a pervasive payment option. In 2026, you can use BNPL to delay and split up payments for anything ranging from a pizza to your rent, and many items in between.  As the market has grown, so has the academic literature. There is now sufficient research into BNPL to take stock and review what we have learned. In this article, we summarize insights from the economics, finance, and marketing academic literature. While we have learned a great deal about BNPL in the last few years, we also discuss many remaining open questions and current concerns impacting policy decisions.   We start by explaining what BNPL products are and the business models of BNPL lenders. Then, we summarize the economics and psychology behind why some consumers use these products. Next, we describe the customer base that uses BNPL. We show the effects of BNPL on consumers, an area of research with substantial policy interest. Another area of policy interest is whether BNPL loans should be reported in a consumer’s credit report. We explain why BNPL is typically not on credit reports and its implications. Finally, we offer some concluding thoughts.

abstract: We study whether model diversity survives selection into trading. In synthetic markets with a fixed mixture of three language-model families, news presentation changes their representation among submitted orders. At the announcement round, Qwen's share of submitted orders shifts by 48 percentage points in the financing event, with little change in net order counts. In the workforce-reduction event, Mistral's share shifts by 40 percentage points while net counts reverse sign. Homogeneous populations remove opposing flow when their active decisions share a direction. An analytical decomposition shows why selection can improve or worsen price accuracy even at unchanged aggregate demand sensitivity. The evidence concerns presentation bundles and submitted flow; cleaner replication and a known-value validation are specified prospectively.

abstract: Many countries require factories to recycle almost all their wastewater and return none to rivers, a standard called zero liquid discharge (ZLD); in India, courts have imposed it on textile and leather clusters. Yet when enforcement tightens, small firms close while larger polluters often endure. This paper asks why, comparing Tirupur, where closures have already occurred, with Kanpur's Jajmau tanneries, where they are ongoing. Small firms depend on shared treatment plants they do not control. As these plants become underused, costs rise, performance declines, and firms with in-house treatment are better able to withstand enforcement. Because compliance is judged by equipment ownership rather than measured discharge, plant failure is attributed to member firms. This final step is the best evidenced, while the earlier links remain suggestive. The paper recommends judging compliance by measured discharge and determining whether the plant or the firm has failed before closure, so enforcement targets pollution rather than the firms least able to absorb it.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

abstract: The pandemic of COVID-19 has transformed the way people live and work, and their willingness to pay for quietness. Using the outbreak of COVID-19 in Singapore as a quasi- natural experiment, we investigate tenants’ changing responses to road traffic noise in the rental housing market, using 46,980 transaction records between 2006 and 2022. By constructing threshold zones by distance to main roads, we first empirically identify treatment vs. control groups in exposure to traffic noise. Second, we use difference-in-differences estimation to show that road traffic noise decreases housing rents by 3.8% in 2020 immediately after the pandemic and rockets to 12.7% in the subsequent year—equivalent to 186.7 US dollars per month. Our results are robust to parallel trend analysis, permutation placebo tests, and tests using alternative distance thresholds or distance to the nearest main road. Third, we adopt a machine learning text analysis of 10,425 rental housing advertisements, showing that tenants’ preference for quietness increases by approximately 10% from 2019 into 2020. The new work-from-home business model and rising traffic from delivery services can explain for this pattern. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper using a large volume of transaction records to quantify city dwellers’ willingness to pay for quietness in the COVID-19 context. Our results have policy implications for nations beyond Singapore and post-pandemic era on the interaction among urban planning, transport networks, and human settlements, and shed light on the pathway to achieve sustainable development goals.

abstract: Forecasting 15-minute Market Clearing Prices in the Indian Energy Exchange Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM) is complicated by pronounced diurnal renewable cycles and frequent upper price-cap events ($10,000\text{ Rs/MWh}$). We propose a leak-safe, cap-aware LightGBM architecture that blends an $L_1$ log-price regressor with an upper-price classifier alongside nine rolling-calibrated quantile heads. Across 257 delivery days (January–September 2026; 24,672 blocks), our baseline model achieves $397.9\text{ Rs/MWh}$ MAE and $171.6\text{ Rs/MWh}$ mean pinball loss, cutting MAE by $31.8\%$ relative to a zero-shot univariate Chronos-2 model ($583.3\text{ Rs/MWh}$) and $32.5\%$ over persistence ($589.1\text{ Rs/MWh}$). On a volatile October–November 2026 holdout, decoupling uncapped price regression from cap classification while adding pre-gate covariates—same-morning real-time prices, prior-day unmatched sell volumes, and capacity-weighted clear-sky solar irradiance—further reduces MAE to $716.0\text{ Rs/MWh}$ versus $2,000.4\text{ Rs/MWh}$ for Chronos-2. Domain-informed covariates within cap-aware boosting drive accuracy gains far more effectively than replacing tabular ensembles with univariate foundation models.

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming economies, societies, and polities, raising fundamental questions about how it should be regulated. Policymakers face choices over whether to prioritize innovation or safety, rely on public oversight or private self-regulation, and govern nationally or internationally. Yet little is known about how citizens evaluate these competing priorities. Here we report a conjoint survey experiment conducted in seven countries with diverse political and economic profiles. We find that citizens strongly support regulating AI and generally prioritize safety over innovation, public governance over private self-regulation, and international over national approaches. The preference for safety is strongest among those who perceive AI as risky, unpredictable, and personally consequential. These findings reveal a systematic misalignment between dominant regulatory approaches and citizen preferences.

abstract: When a robot practices without human resets, every attempt still costs wall-clock time, actuator wear, and sometimes a person's attention, yet the schedulers that decide what to practice next treat attempts as free. We present an open, low-cost testbed for measuring these costs: a self-built SO-101 arm runs two demonstration-trained ACT policies that reset each other, with a vision-based success detector and a ledger that records the time, joint travel, and human interventions of every attempt. We formulate cost-aware practice scheduling, in which task selection is rewarded by measured competence gain net of embodied cost, and specify in advance the comparison that will test it. Its first two conditions, run on hardware for 51 minutes of robot time, show that a fixed retry limit did not reduce the share of execution time lost to failures (36%, against 27% for a feasibility rule; not significant) and saved no robot time. The logs suggest why: failures showed no sign of clustering, so a retry right after a failure was as likely to succeed as any other attempt. The ledger also shows that most of the retry rule's extra human time came from cubes knocked out of reach rather than from the rule itself, and a cost-aware rule replayed on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit. We also report lessons from building the system, including a coverage effect in which concentrating demonstrations in a smaller workspace raised success there from 8/20 to 10/10.

We also report lessons from building the system, including a coverage effect in which concentrating demonstrations in a smaller workspace raised success there from 8/20 to 10/10.

abstract: Trust can attract fraud when it delays verification. We develop a two-market signaling model in which generative AI lowers fabrication, verification, and targeting costs. In the single-market benchmark, fabrication begins before verification becomes worthwhile. Claim credibility therefore falls when fabrication starts and recovers once checking begins. Across markets, deception is initially rarer in the higher-quality market, so verification starts later there. Cheaper targeting then draws mobile deceptive sellers into this higher-quality but less vigilant market. Their entry can push the market's transaction integrity below that of a lower-quality market that already verifies. The inflow eventually triggers verification and deters further entry. We call this mechanism trust arbitrage. In the age of generative AI, trust can thus create an endogenous protection gap that redirects deception across markets.

abstract: Prediction-market shares differ from traditional financial products in that, with no information or outside utility, classical delta-neutral Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) market making cannot be financed by payoff-uninformative noise flow. Transaction-level evidence from a major prediction-market CLOB platform shows makers profiting not from spread but from carrying an underpriced side to settlement-the empirical signature of behavioral tail demand rather than classical, randomized noise. We build this tail demand directly into the model and study an LMSR and a CLOB on the same event. A pre-shock CLOB quote inside the common-signal band is picked off; competitive quotes therefore screen informed traders out of the book. CLOB makers earn screening rent by carrying the underpriced side to resolution, while informed flow routes to the LMSR. The venues coexist: the CLOB supplies the tail-demand rent margin that lets the LMSR recover part of its loss to informed flow, and AMM depth moves the CLOB premium with a sign set by maker-side contestability-widening it where standing quotes can be undercut, compressing it where a committed maker carries the book. With three or more outcomes, binary-book CLOBs pin switch prices but leave implied beliefs indeterminate, whereas the LMSR prices the outcome simplex coherently and uses collateral more efficiently.

abstract: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free façade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20° or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20°), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1–9.0° on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70–0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20° it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to façades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12–45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and façade-level data reproduce the main results. CASAS.ES also publishes the article and its methodology .
